utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And first of all, the Chamber -- I apologise for the late start but a traffic jam caused me a delay of more than 30 minutes this morning. I highly regret. We have a housekeeping session today. I see Mr. Harmon and Mr. Margetts present for the Prosecution, and Mr. Stewart and Mr. Josse for the Defence assisted by their team members. An agenda was distributed yesterday among the parties. Did you receive those -- the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we have, Your Honour, on the Defence side, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is one point to add [French coming over English channel]. But I think it's already corrected. There is one point to add in relation to what is now under item 15. We will come to that at a later stage. The agenda. Point 1, exhibits of which we now have received translations and where we have received no objections regarding their admission, and that is, I slowly read, Prosecution P954, P968, P969, P971 to P973, P975 to P978, P992, P1009 to 1011, P1017 to P1019, P1034, P1050, P1051, P1054, P1058, P1061 to P1064, P1067 to P1071. Defence exhibits D100, D130 to D132, D136, D137 and D140. Whenever I said "to," that would include the second number. Any matters to be raised? If not, the Chamber will decide to admit these exhibits into evidence. I do not hear anything from the parties which means that the exhibits I just mentioned are now admitted into evidence. There are still a number of exhibits which are waiting for translation or for completion of the translation provided until now. That's Prosecution P970, P1072, and P1073. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have completed the translations of P970 and 1073 and we are prepared to distribute those this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: P1072 is still in translation and we are not prepared to -- on that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Defence will have an opportunity until next Tuesday, to raise any objections against P970 and P1073. Then Defence exhibits, D84, D106, D113, D114, D123, D133, D138, D139 and last one, D141. Mr. Stewart. Or Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Primarily I'm dealing with these matters, Your Honour. Secondly, as Your Honour can see, Mr. Stewart is having some technical difficulties with his LiveNote reception. Your Honour, the Defence aren't in a position to inform the Court when these translations will be ready for filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any news about them or you just gave them for translation and didn't see them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure some have been done. In fairness, I have not asked the person on our team who is responsible for marrying up B/C/S with English, just to oversee that task. I'm happy for the Court to impose some sort of time limit to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence is invited to inform by e-mail Chamber staff about any document which -- of which the translation is by now ready. And also inform whether the translation has been provided to the Prosecution by -- I would say just inventory by tomorrow, close of business.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would be Friday, 4.00. Then the next item on the agenda is the dates for Prosecution exhibits. Yes, I think it's mainly a matter of putting it on the record. These are the two, what I understand 1994 interviews. That's P1012 and P1013. I think that information it is already available but it's not yet on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were in contact with BBC. BBC informed us that in respect of the interview of Mr. Krajisnik, Prosecution Exhibit 1012, the date of the interview was 21 September 1994. In respect of P1013, the interview of Mr. Izetbegovic, the date of the interview was 4 October 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The information coming from a well-known British broadcasting organisation, is there any need for the Defence to further -- then the Registrar is instructed to add these dates as the dates of the interview on the exhibit list, and I do understand the dates are not challenged by the Defence. Then we come to -- the next item is the admission of Exhibit P1008. We needed some time for the translation and then there was some e-mail exchange in which Mr. Josse, I think you already expressed to us your view that you might be late with any other objection apart from objections caused by the translation. Did --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I did basically concede that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That is true. Could I make this observation? I'm not saying it's not there. I was unable to find the passage in the transcript where the admissibility of this document had been discussed, and then raised. If I'm wrong about that I'm certainly not going to waste any more time on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the only matter ever raised was about translations not being available. I have a full list of the transcripts sources on the matter if you could like to consult them, I could even consider to -- but then I have to first to review whether there are any notes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the Chamber is inclined to say that you're late with any other objections but before giving a final decision during the first break the Chamber staff will provide you with all the relevant numbers and, to the extent possible, with copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would be grateful. I undoubtedly raised a concern at the time the exhibit was first put to the witness in question. My second observation is the objection that is I wish to make now will take no more than a minute. So perhaps the Court would bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One minute, I think it would add to the fair administration of justice, so unless Mr. Harmon you would oppose, we would grant that one minute to Mr. Josse. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the e-mail correspondence that Your Honour is referring to I alluded to two grounds. In fact, realistically I'm only pursuing one and that is ground that the Court will hear me repeat on a number of occasions in relation to a number of documents today. This document was put to the witness. The witness was not in a position to confirm or for that matter to deny the veracity of any of its contents. Therefore, Your Honour, in my submission it can't be admitted because the witness simply was unable to assist as to the truth of its contents in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the witness confirmed that the document originated from the organisation he was working for?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. That was Mr. Harmon's assertion that this had come from the association. The witness knew nothing about that. He, like the Defence, was prepared to accept what Mr. Harmon says about that. That came out rather worse than it was meant to. We, of course, accept Mr. Harmon's assertion that it came from that particular association but that doesn't help the matter at all, I contend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour the only other objection that I recall raising is this particular exhibit was there was no proper showing as to how the data was collected, from whom, by which methods, et cetera. I have informed the Court and the Court officer and the Defence by e-mail the manner in which it was collected. I referred the Court to the testimony of a witness from that organisation who testified over one or two pages as to how they collected that data. That was the objection that was made at the time and that was then referred to counsel specifically, those passages, so we are prepared to stand on that information as to the reliability of the information provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I made clear, in my e-mail there were two grounds. That was the second ground of objection. I'm not pursuing that. I accept what Mr. Harmon says, not necessarily accept that what he's saying in that regard is the truth but I'm prepared to concede that it's sufficient for the admission of the document. My grounds are a different one, that is the witness simply couldn't shed any light object the document at all, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then it would not necessarily be inadmissible evidence but it would then perhaps be an exhibit which is introduced but then perhaps not appropriately done so through the witness but could be introduced by other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that's an issue that the Court is going to have to grapple with later on in the agenda, and I'm going to make some submissions about them in general but that is -- as a broad proposition that is a possibility, I accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where I allowed you to further expound on the -- on your objections that did not automatically include that we -- that the Chamber has considered the objection as being done in due time. So we have the two matters. First of all, whether there is still -- whether you're late or not and then second if you're not late then we have heard your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well I'm grateful for being allowed the minute or so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's P1008. Let's move on and the next issue is that the Defence has expressed its intention to oppose the admission of quite a number of Prosecution exhibits introduced through the -- during the testimony of the Witness Savkic. I mentioned the numbers P1055 to P1057, P1059, P1060, P1065 and P1066. I'd like to give an opportunity to the Defence to raise the objection and to make submissions in that respect it deems useful. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Starting with P1055, when this was put to the witness, not only did he deny any knowledge of it but he said unequivocally that it was a forgery. That raises the issue as to its provenance but even if its provenance was demonstrated by the Prosecution, that is, they were able to show where they found it, by whom, in what circumstances, so on and so forth, which there is not a jot of evidence in relation to at this particular juncture. Even if they were able to demonstrate that the Defence would still maintain this objection bearing in mind the witness again said it was a forgery and he was, I repeat, unable to shed any light on it at all save for the fact it was simply not true. So far as P1056 is concerned, I actually have the reference for that in the transcript. At about page 20667, the witness denied any knowledge of that document or its contents. So the point that I've already made in relation, for example, to P1008 applies here. The same applies in the Defence submission to P1057. My note says that that is found at page 20676 of the transcript. So far as P1059 was concerned, again, the witness said he had no knowledge of the document, he didn't even acknowledge that that particular document was genuine. And it therefore goes that bit further. So far as P1060 is concerned, the witness said he had no knowledge of its contents or of its accuracy. That's found at approximately page 20684. So far as P1065 is concerned, that appears at the evidence at page 20697. The witness said that that too was a forgery, the same two points apply, forgery, lack of knowledge. And so far as P1066 is concerned, which is found at page 20703, the witness denied any knowledge of the contents of the document and indeed didn't accept the truth of the contents. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Harmon? Or Mr. Margetts, I see you're on your feet so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honours will recall this particular witness and you will recall that we put a number of documents to this witness, some of which the Defence are contesting and some of which they are not contesting. It is our submission that in regard to each of the Prosecution exhibits we put to this witness, the witness failed to deal with those documents either credibly or reliably or in any adequate manner. The documents that the Defence object to are a sample of those documents that the witness failed to deal with. The general manner in which the Defence has dealt with those documents, and the reaction of the witness to those documents, can be, with the greatest of respect to my learned friend, improved upon. It is not the fact in respect of Appeals Chamber of these that he denied knowledge of the contents of many of them. In fact some of his comments authenticated the content. Well, corroborated the events described in them, and accordingly this corroboration can be utilised for the authentication of the document. I'll deal with each of the documents in turn. The first document was Exhibit P1055 and I don't know whether Your Honours have the advantage of that document being before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have them in front of me but that's the document, the first one, about the -- that's the fake document according to the witness in which the monetary streams are -- it's the unsigned document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a document that -- first of all, it was the witness's position which was expressed very clearly at pages 20602, of the transcript, that the Crisis Staff never existed, never functioned. Furthermore, the witness said that he was never a member of the Crisis Staff or was never informed he was, and asked to detail his positions that he held throughout the relevant period, at pages 20634 to pages 20637, furthermore and pages 20644 through to pages 20646, he failed to include the position of president of the Crisis Staff as one of those positions he held. This document directly impeached him on a critical matter. Now, this document didn't stand alone. Other documents that we produced corroborated the existence of the Crisis Staff. In fact the other documents the Defence object to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, if I just may interrupt you, the position of the Defence and position of the witness in relation to 1055 is that it's a forgery. Does a forgery -- if it's true that it's a forgery, it could well be -- this document could well be understood as corroborating the witness's evidence that the Crisis Staff never existed because documents that are produced are forgeries. If, however, the -- it's -- it very much depends on whether it's a forgery, yes or no. If it's a forgery then it might support the witness views. If it's not a forgery, it's -- well, it is likely to corroborate the Prosecution's view. But you're now presenting it as it should be admitted because it demonstrates that the witness was not telling us the truth when the Crisis Staff -- that the Crisis Staff did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We say that that is a relevant matter to be taken into account, in light of the totality of this witness's evidence and the Court's opportunity to assess his demeanour, and his reaction to this document, the Court is in a position to assess why that reaction was so vehement and the nature of that reaction but I'll deal with the issue of how the witness alleged it was a forgery and we say on its face the manner in which he dealt with it demonstrated that that allegation had no substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is it for the witness to demonstrate that it's a forgery or is it for the Prosecution to demonstrate that it's an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well in our submission the Defence is relying on this witness's evidence that it was a forgery and in our submission the Court can reject that evidence because of the various factors that I'll be pleased if I could enumerate before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Those factors are that the first thing was that he asserted that the substance of the document was to alleviate an obligation to a republican authority for tax liability. There is no logical sense in that. First of all the document on its face was about directing funds received to the municipal assembly budget so it appeared on its face to be an internal document not directed to a third party's liability. The second point on that issue is that the document was merely a municipal level document. A municipal body cannot in any way affect a liability to a republican organ and accordingly any obligation to a republican organ would still subsist regardless of this document so the document did not establish what he said it established. Thirdly we've had the opportunity of reviewing exhibit P52. One of the people whom this witness said had persecuted his life was the author of P52, and Your Honours will recall that's a facsimile from a Mr. Rajko Dukic to Mr. Krajisnik and to Mr. Karadzic wherein Mr. Rajko Dukic at paragraph 2 details the aid he has provided, the contributions he has made, and the discharge of his taxation liability to the republican authorities. Thirdly, he says that this was done in order to be a credible document, a forgery that was meant to affect a belief in those that read it that in fact there had been a genuine change of the obligations of parties obliged to pay tax. It does not make sense that the person who made that forgery would refer to a body that did not exist at the time, to perpetrate that forgery because the error in the document would be immediately apparent and its lack of authenticity would immediately apparent. And remember that was the critical issue we were discussing, whether or not the Crisis Staff existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts may I take it that the second time you said thirdly that you meant fourthly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, my apologies. My notes only detail four points, one of the initial points occurred to me whilst I was on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you refresh my memory. You're now saying that it's -- the testimony of the witness is illogic. Did you put all these -- all the illogical parts and it's not clearly in my mind anymore to the witness to the witness which would be appropriate to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The situation was this, Your Honour. When the witness was initially confronted with this document he was given ample opportunity to clarify why he said it was a forgery and I -- and memory serves me -- if memory serves me correctly, Your Honour in fact questioned him to gain clarity as to why he said it was a forgery and at page 20659 of the transcript, Your Honour concluded that it was unclear to you still what he was attempting to allege, yet that you invited me to proceed with the examination and I did so also indicating to the Court that the explanation did not make sense despite the time afforded to the witness to explain it. Secondly a long discussion about there allegation proceeded at pages 20775 through to pages 20778 whereupon Your Honour again undertook the questioning to clarify what it was this witness was trying to allege. At the end of that questioning, Your Honour said, "Yes, well, now, it is clear to me what you're saying." And in that circumstance, it wasn't in our view going to assist matters or to attempt to clarify it further. The witness was given ample opportunity on two occasions to put specifically, to explain very clearly to the Court what he was saying. At that stage we accepted he had done so fully and with full opportunity and despite these logical inconsistencies we didn't see that it would be beneficial at that stage to pursue the issue further. So any way, the other issue that he rose was the stamp on the document and that was he said it was inappropriate for the municipal authorities to -- the stamp of the municipal authority to be on a Crisis Staff document. In our submission, Your Honours have received evidence that that in fact is an appropriate stamp, given that the Crisis Staff step into, so to speak, the shoes of the municipal assembly when they're exercising their functions. So that's our submission on the allegation it's a forgery. We say it doesn't make sense. On its face it can be disregarded. It was a desperate effort for -- made by this witness to escape from a document that directly impeached him. The provenance of this document, Your Honour, is that it was delivered to the Office of the Prosecutor by a representative of the Republika Srpska government in October 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I take objection to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My learned friend can't start making statements like that without giving some notice to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was on my mind, Mr. Margetts, to ask you whether you had provided this information to the Defence, because if the Defence wants to challenge that or to not to challenge that they should at least know what the origin of these documents in the view of the Prosecution is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have submissions in regard to the provenance in relation to each of the documents that are listed that have been objected to and we had intended to present that material to the Court today. Obviously, we apologise for not having done so at an earlier opportunity, and given the Defence an ability to respond to that. So it may be better if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To delay that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: To delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be -- Mr. Josse, at least, the least Mr. Margetts could offer, I take it, in your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect I agree with that. I've had issues of this sort with Mr. Harmon in the past. He has provided me with the information and I've withdrawn that aspect of objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I expect, Mr. Margetts, that you'll inform Mr. Josse in full on the provenance of these documents prior to raising the matter again and informing the Chamber and then we'll learn whether there is any challenge by the Defence of the provenance of these documents. Yes. Mr. Margetts, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take it then that we will have further submissions on those documents once the Defence has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we could do is we could for the time being say that we now invite Mr. Josse to comment on what you said, apart from the provenance part, and because part of it was the totality of the documents, the logic of it, but if Mr. Josse would prefer to delay those responses as well to after a moment where he has been informed about the provenance, I would give him leave to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would take that option, in conjunction with a preference to reply to my learned friend's objections as a whole after he's been through all these various documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we first wait until you, Mr. Margetts, have provided Mr. Josse with the information on the provenance of the documents and then we will hear from Mr. Josse his response to your response to the objection in its totality rather than in split up portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So, if I may, Your Honour, other than the issue of provenance I'm in a position to put the position of the Prosecution regarding each of the other documents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps it's good that we hear it and Mr. Josse will take his time to answer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would be very grateful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- the second document was exhibit P1056, you recall the issues that that document addressed. This was a document dated the 30th of May 1992 and it was a document signed by a gentleman, Lalovic, who was, according to the evidence of the witness, the president of the municipal assembly. This document abolished the Crisis Staff and replaced the Crisis Staff with a military command and a War Presidency. This document again directly impeached the witness and I point to the impeachment for the purpose of saying, well, this was the motivation what -- that was behind the witness's attempt to escape from the impact of this document. It impeached the witness because, again, it showed that there was a Crisis Staff functioning, a Crisis Staff that was in fact abolished. It impeached the witness because the witness had failed to acknowledge that a War Presidency had taken over the conduct of the municipality and alleged to the contrary that the municipal assembly had been the functioning and authoritative body, and I again refer to pages 20062 of the transcript. Mr. Josse's submitted that the witness denied knowledge of this document or its content; not the case. At pages 20602 prior to this document being presented, the witness had said the Crisis Staff was abolished on the 30th of May 1992. In other words, he volunteered express knowledge of the contents of this document. Furthermore, when presented with this document he didn't doubt its authenticity. He said in fact Mr. Lalovic was a bureaucrat and he abolished something that had never existed. Again, we point to the illogic of that explanation by the witness. We also have a submission in regard to the provenance of that document. In regard to Exhibit P1057, again, the witness denied knowledge of this document. There was no reason he should have had knowledge of the document. This was a report of 27 May 1992, that -- once again contrary to the Defence's submissions he did not deny knowledge of the content of this document. This document was a report to the chief of police of the Milici police station and the document addressed the issue of the sabotage or the attack on a convoy that was driving from the Boksit mine through Konjevic Polje. The attack on the convoy occurred on the 27th of May, 1992, and the witness gave evidence to that effect. At pages 20561 through to 20564 of the transcript, specifically citing an incident at page 20564, so accordingly the witness's evidence corroborated this document as to date and event. The witness's, we say, feeble attempt to escape the implications of this document was to say, well, where it says a report about this event was made to the Crisis Staff, that's a mistake. They meant something else. The fact is that the three documents we've just referred to do refer to the existence of a Crisis Staff, do corroborate each other and do directly impeach the witness and his vain attempts to escape the impact of that impeachment resulted in the illogical and unfounded evidence he gave in relation to these documents. The next document was Exhibit P1059. The witness again was directly impeached. The witness was asked by Defence counsel what occurred after the 14th of April 1992, when he, according to him, left the Vlasenica city after the negotiations as he described them had not succeeded. And he was asked, "When did the violence in the municipality break out?" His answer was the violence broke out when there was sabotages on the roads from 21 May 1992. Your Honour correctly interjected and said to him, well, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that a takeover took place, that there was a JNA unit, that there were -- there was actually military action in the municipality on the evening of the 20th, morning of the 21st of April 1992. Now, he didn't acknowledge that happened. This document that was presented to him was a retrospective account from a member of the 1st Vlasenica Infantry Brigade that detailed in fact that the Crisis Staff had in conjunction with the JNA deployed units that were involved in the takeover of the city. The witness consistent with his efforts to avoid mentioning this issue in his examination-in-chief simply said that's not correct. He didn't doubt the authenticity of the document. He just disputed the fact that the events described therein had occurred in the manner that they are described there and in the manner that witnesses or evidence that's been received by this Court corroborates. Again, we have a submission on the provenance of the document. The next document is P1060. And this was a document dated 8 December 1992, and it was a document that set out the minutes of a meeting of the War Presidency of Milici. So we've dealt with that issue before. He didn't acknowledge the existence of a War Presidency. This document directly impeached him. Later in his evidence, he sought to avoid in what we said -- what we say was a very clumsy manner the fact that he it was the commander of a battalion and this document clearly set out that there were two battalions in existence at December 1992, the Derventa Battalion and the Milici Battalion, and again this document impeached him on his evidence regarding to the existence of those battalions. So again, he was motivated to avoid the impact of this document. Now, again it's not the case that his evidence doesn't in a manner assist the Court in arriving at a conclusion as to the authenticity of this document. His Honour Judge Hanoteau questioned the witness at page 20685 as to whether he was aware of problems with commander Petkovic which was the major subject of this document. The witness said yes he was aware of the problems with commander Petkovic that were described in this document. So he actually corroborated the content of this document and we say that that can assist the Court in establishing the authenticity of this document. Furthermore, Exhibits P892, Ewan Brown tab 13.1, and P892, Ewan Brown tab 14, corroborate the existence of a battalion known as the Milici Battalion, and again impeached this witness and again corroborate the -- this document and its authenticity. Again, we have submissions on the provenance of this document. Document P1065 addresses the witness's broad and sweeping evidence as to what occurred in the municipality of Milici and the surrounds in Vlasenica and Srebrenica. This evidence is set out at pages 20572 through to 20583 of the transcript, and fails to acknowledge that any crimes at all were perpetrated against Muslim victims and refers in a -- in our submission, a biased and unhelpful way, to reports composed by the Serb chief of police Rade Bilanovic in regard to Serb -- incidents where there were Serb victims and charges that were to be brought against the Muslim commander, Naser Oric. In this context the witness was asked questions in relation to the Susica camp which was a massive enterprise and the Court has received evidence in relation to it. The witness, whilst not being consistent, claimed that he didn't have knowledge of the Susica camp at the time it existed. But at pages 20697 of the transcript he slipped up. He said, I myself didn't ask at that time as to what -- how many prisoners were in the Susica camp. Your Honour asked a follow-up -- Your Honour, president of the Court asked a follow-up question in relation to that to which he backed away from what had already been a statement relating to his contemporaneous knowledge of the camp. In that context, the Exhibit P1065 was put to him showing that 800 persons in this small area were in fact detained in the Susica camp and we say that that document, by its very nature and substance, impeaches the witness in regard to his knowledge of that camp. Secondly, also under the command of the brigade that he was subordinate to. In our submission there were a large number of people detained in Zvornik who were subsequently massacred. This report referred to those people, and we put it to him that he knew of the -- those people as well. This document doesn't stand alone. We have other exhibits which corroborate this document, P872 and P874 also referred to a massive number of people, 650 and 600 respectively detained in the Susica camp in June 1992. Furthermore, Exhibit P678 again corroborates the information that was contained in this document relating to the VR's involvement in the detention of the people in Zvornik. Again we have a submission in regard to the provenance of that document. The final document that was addressed by the Defence was Exhibit P1066. This is an order for the cleansing of the enemy from the areas of Birac dated 7 June 1992. Again I refer to the witness's evidence at pages 20572 to 20583 where he provided, as I say in our submission, a biased account of what was occurring in the area and failed to mention that there were proactive cleansing operations being conducted by the East Bosnia Corps and the units that he was involved with. He doubted the authenticity of this document. We say that the document and the cleansing orders are corroborated by Exhibits P874 and P892, tabs 13.1 and 14, and also the orders that we've seen from the commander Svetozar Andric of 28 May 1992 and 31 May 1992, and we again say that this was a self-interested denial which had no credibility. He in the course of his evidence at pages 20577 to 20578 said that all Serb villages were burnt down and all the population that Muslims could possibly slaughter were slaughtered. He was questioned by Your Honour at pages 20580 to 20581 in relation to whether there were investigations in relation to crimes against the Muslim population. He sought desperately to avoid an answer to Your Honour's questions, and eventually it can be made out that he wasn't -- he said there were criminal charges regardless of whether there were Muslim or Serb casualties. Quite clearly these documents show a positive campaign by the Serb army to cleanse these villages and areas of Muslims and we say that impeaches the witness. Again we have a submission on the provenance of that document and we will notify the Defence in due course. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. Mr. Josse, may I take it that you would save your response for a later moment or if there is -- is there anything you would like to immediately now already submit to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. I'll reserve the Defence's position, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may. Then we move to our -- now we move to the next item on the agenda which is the documentation regarding the death of Husein Hotic, a Muslim from Japra Valley, and the Chamber asked for further information, and we have -- we understand that the Defence opposes the introduction of the documentation that has been gathered now by Mr. Harmon. Mr. Harmon, would it not be a good idea that before we invite to you provide this information, to first hear from Mr. Josse what the objections are and then see whether the objections are of a kind which would not even require the Chamber to look to the documents or whether we would perhaps pursue the matter further and receive the documentation in order to decide on the admissibility of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm satisfied to proceed that way. I could summarise briefly if Your Honours wish what we have done and what we have prepared and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, what I'd like to avoid is that in your presentation, that already a lot of information comes to us if we would decide at a later stage to the objections by Mr. Josse should result in not gaining any knowledge of it. So therefore I'd briefly invite Mr. Josse first of all to explain to us the nature of his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They are basically procedural, Your Honour, rather than substantive. I reserve the Defence position so far as the substantive issues are concerned. Mr. Harmon has been very helpful, if I may say, in this regard, and he will correct me if I'm wrong but in relation to these Hotic documents, I think they have only been provided in B/C/S to the Defence. But I'll be corrected if I'm wrong on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct and I also provided the Defence a summary that I was provided, I provided an oral summary of their contents to Mr. Josse as well so he and I sit in the same position. We have B/C/S documents. They have been looked at by my interpreters. I had provided Mr. Josse with a summary of the contents and I gave them to him so that he could confer with his language assistants as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make it clear, Your Honour, that were the Court really against the submission I'm going to make now, then, of course, the issue of substance is one that I reserve, albeit, frankly, I suspect that will not detain the Court very long. But our fundamental objection, and it's the real objection, is the way this is being done. This is not, we contend, the point in the case for the Prosecution to adduce more evidence because that is what the Prosecution are seeking to do. They wish to put before the Court evidence in the middle of the Defence case. The Rules, we submit, do not provide for that eventuality. Common sense, we submit, do not provide for that eventuality. And we contend the Rules do provide, and common sense for that matter provides an appropriate time for the Prosecution to do this, and that is at a later stage in the case. By the same token, the difficulty with the exercise that my learned friend wishes to undertake, and it illustrates the very point, the procedural point that I'm making, is how is this going to be done? Presumably, a significant number of documents, but for this purpose in fact it doesn't matter whether it's one or more documents, are going to be handed to the Court, and, of course, be translated because they've got to be, but the Defence can't challenge them, the Defence can't cross-examine anyone about them, the Defence can't do anything other than to say, we do accept the documents, we don't accept the documents. That frankly would be comment any way. And in my submission, this is a completely inappropriate procedure to adopt at this particular juncture of the case and the Court shouldn't countenance it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, first off, the issue of Mr. Hotic was not raised by the Prosecutor in its examination of this witness. I will direct Your Honour's and counsel's attention to pages 19707 through 19711. The context in which the Hotic murder came up was when Mr. Josse was asking questions of his witness and he was referring to an interview of Mr. Pasic that had been specifically taken earlier, prior to the proceedings, and specifically he asked questions -- he quoted from the interview by Mr. Resch asking him about the murder of Husein Hotic. And then Pasic then claimed to the murder of Husein Hotic rebutted the proposition that there had been no proceedings had taken place where Serb perpetrators had not been punished and he, Mr. Pasic, said there was a record of that trial, and he used the word "trial.". At 19711, lines 18 through 23, Your Honour Judge Orie stated that you were very much interested in the events of the Japra Valley and asked where Husein Hotic was killed. Now, following -- so the Prosecution didn't attempt to lead the evidence of Husein Hotic. It was clearly a result of questions that were asked by Mr. Josse, and then the Court made an inquiry, and we, following that inquiry by the Court, made efforts to and did obtain, we contacted the president of the basic court in Novi Grad, and obtained the file. And we are in a position to answer Your Honour's specific question as to where Husein Hotic was killed. I have not had these documents translated. As I say I have given them to my colleagues from the Defence so they could review them. The procedural point is that the Court in our submission can ask for any evidence it wants at any time it wants and the parties should be in a position to assist the Court if it is so directed. It's our submission that we were directed through the inquiry of the Court, to find out the answer to that question. And we have endeavoured to do so. We have done so. And we are prepared to introduce that evidence that was the result of, as I say, precipitated by the questions of Mr. Josse, the answers of the Defence witness, and, as I say, Your Honour, these -- this matter, we can answer the question, we have -- the complete file. I can summarise the contents of the file. I won't do so unless I'm directed to at this moment. That is our submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Josse, Mr. Harmon responded to your argument that the Prosecution is now presenting any further evidence whereas it also is my recollection that the Court wanted to find out, could serve several evidentiary purposes to find out what actually happened on matters the witness described. And we asked, I think we did not immediately rely upon Rule 98 but we asked the Prosecution to further explore whether there was material which could assist the Chamber, and if not, presented by one of the parties, could be -- by the Chamber could ask that material to be produced. That's one issue I'd like to hear your comment on. The second issue is that you say what can the Defence do? Well, let me just raise a few suggestions. The Defence could challenge the authenticity of the documents and either ask leave to call further witnesses to further explore that matter or to invite the Court to ask for further details on the provenance of these documents. Or even suggest to the Court that, if the Court is interested to look at these documents, that since the Defence has its doubts on authenticity, that it invites the Chamber also to ask for the production of further evidence on the authenticity. I mean, there are a lot of ways I think, technical ways, in dealing with it. So therefore where you're more or less helpless and what could the Defence do any more, I would trigger your inventiveness and see whether you would agree with me that there is no reason yet to raise your hands in feeling totally helpless. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour's last paragraph, as it appears in LiveNote is very helpful, if I may respectfully say, and one that the Defence, I'm sure, will consider extremely carefully in relation to authenticity, the possibility of calling further witnesses to explore the matter. That's an issue that I'll discuss both with Mr. Stewart and indeed with Mr. Krajisnik in due course. So far as the procedural is concerned, and I appreciate that this Court may not want to get too heavily bogged down in the Rules, we contend that Rule 85 is clear as to the presentation of Rule 98 evidence. It sets out the presentation of evidence as, in the following sequence, one, evidence for the Prosecution, 2, evidence for the Defence, 3 Prosecution evidence in rebuttal, 4, Defence evidence in rejoinder and then, 5, evidence ordered by the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 98. And in our submission, Rule 98 material only applies at that stage of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me that the heading of Rule 85(A) says that unless otherwise directed by the Trial Chamber in the interests of justice, evidence at the trial shall be presented in the following sequence? Because then I would really like you to go to the substance of it. I mean, we hear the evidence of a witness on whether or not investigations in relation to the death of Mr. Hotic were conducted -- I mean that's an issue at that moment. Should we now -- is it really your submission that the Chamber should now -- well, of course, unless you say at this moment, of course, we'll come with a lot of evidence on that matter so please wait for a while, but the Chamber, of course, now and then seeks to form its opinion on matters of reliability and credibility not only by hearing witness A says this, Witness B says that, but also to see whether there is any source by which you can verify the, or at least to make a better assessment, to form a better opinion on the credibility and the reliability. For example, just to give you one example, if you ask yourself what you can see from a certain point, of course, you could call five witnesses and say, "I can see from point A, a church," I can -- the next one says, "you can't see that." Of course, very often a photograph will be very helpful to see what you can see from point A or from point B or what you can't see. So therefore, the Chamber is aware of -- that witnesses may make mistakes, that witnesses may not have a full knowledge of every detail of something they did not -- dealt with personally that's true, for Defence witnesses, that's true for Prosecution witnesses, and seeks then further material which can assist it in forming its opinion on reliability and credibility of the witness. Is it really your submission that, apart from whether you would like to come back to this point and the Chamber did not have that impression until now, that we should wait until the very, very end to ask the parties to see whether there is any material which could assist the Chamber in this way or would you consider it possible that the Chamber would direct otherwise under Rule 85, in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that this morning we have a tendency to put matters off but the issues that Your Honour has just raised in my opinion, using the word "opinion" I hope advisedly are of real procedural importance. It's an issue I would like to discuss with Mr. Stewart. We have discussed the matter briefly prior to the submission I first made this morning but I would like to consult with him further if I would be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'll have an opportunity to do so. Mr. Josse, perhaps we could use the next break for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps if there is anything Mr. Harmon would like to raise now so that you can include that in your further consultations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The only thing is, Your Honour, the next break we are both -- we need to have a consultation with our client about item 15 on the agenda because we haven't had the reports prior to this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We received them relatively late as well, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And one is not in my client's language so we've already earmarked that time to go and see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps it's not of such an urgency but I'll first give an opportunity to Mr. Harmon to raise whatever he wants to raise in this respect so that you can include that in your further internal discussions and second I'd like to know from Mr. Harmon, since he's working on the basis of a summary, how much material is there? Are we talking about 20 pages, 100 pages or 500 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's why I was holding this file in my hands. I'll display it to the Court. I would say it's 45 to 50 pages, and that was going to be the point of my question. I have given this to the Defence sometime ago so they could examine. I have identified the source of this to the Defence. I have had an opportunity to inform them of the conclusions that we have reached based on the interpretation. I don't particularly care to have this much work done by the language assistants if counsel and I can agree that certain facts are evident in this particular file. So my suggestion, Your Honour, would be that counsel had this for a considerable period of time before I embarked on having this whole file translated, that we see if we can reach a number of agreed facts from it and certainly, the fact that Your Honour inquired about, where Mr. Hotic was killed, is clear. It's revealed in this file. So perhaps we can approach it in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Josse, the Chamber gives you an opportunity to further consult on the matter with Mr. Stewart. There is another matter. If either on the basis of the position the Defence will take after the consultations, or if the Chamber would order the Prosecution to provide the Chamber with the information, the Chamber would like you also very much to see if there is any way of agreeing with the Prosecution on the content of that material. I mean, the questions are clear. The Chamber wants to see to what extent there is material which supports or does not support the evidence of the witness Pasic. And the Chamber -- I mean, we know that if you're talking about court proceedings, that you get a lot of other stuff in it which, of course, is not the core interest of the Chamber to know. So would you please then include in your conversation with Mr. Stewart also the practical way of dealing with the matter, which could be that there is an agreed summary of the core content of this material, as far as relevance, in relation to the questions the Chamber raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I assure the court that we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea when you could -- perhaps there is even a second break. I do not know. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would quite like to try and resolve this matter this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we also could -- I mean usually the first break is half an hour. We could have -- we perhaps could make the break longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Great minds think alike, Your Honour. Mr. Stewart said exactly the same to me at the moment Your Honour was uttering those words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then we'll hear from you at a later stage this morning. We are close at the moment to a break but let's just see whether there is -- yes, then we have the, I would say, although not exactly the same but the parties were invited to meet and to see whether they could agree on a method of introducing the evidence on Prosecution's -- in Court of Novi Grad and Banja Luka. An agreement could not be reached and the Chamber would now like to hear from the parties briefly their objections or their opinions on, positive opinions, on admission of that evidence. Let's take the same procedure here again that we will first hear from you, Mr. Josse, that you first explain to us the basics of your objection and then to see whether we should ask the Prosecution to provide us with the material before making a final determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I rise, Your Honour, because I think I stand to be corrected by Mr. Harmon, the issue is identical, absolutely identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Absolutely identical. Yes. Here the same, the Judges asked for it so you say identical, that's the issue that under Rule 85, evidence called by the Chamber should be -- it's also a matter for you to discuss with Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear. Then we'll hear from you after perhaps a prolonged break. Unless there's any matter, Mr. Harmon, you would like to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think the procedural point is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we'll hear from you. Perhaps we try to finish the agenda on part A, then have the break, and then move on to part B, other matters on the agenda. For the next agenda item, that's agenda item 8, we should turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. First of all I would like to ask Mr. Josse and Mr. Stewart whether the -- their conversation has changed in any way, I would say, the 98/85 issue that is evidence requested by the Chamber, and Mr. Josse, perhaps there is no need but since it also covers number -- let me see, I think it's number 8 on the agenda, I'd like you to take care that nothing is said which would violate any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't spend a lot of time on the issue, for reasons I've already explained. Our discussion indicated that we would like to have another opportunity to discuss it before I make further submissions to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So at the next break would be convenient for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there will be a next break. Perhaps there will be a short break. Yes, we'll grant you that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we continue with the agenda. We are now in part B. Mr. Harmon, item 9 on the agenda deals with that portion of the testimony which told about an attack on a convoy. Could you please inform the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I became aware of this issue when I got the agenda. I looked at the transcript last night and I am in a position to inform the Court that we do have videos that we will provide to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the Defence could decide whether they want to use that video, and I take it then since it's your video that it could be introduced even without recalling Mr. Mikic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's fine. Or it could be introduced by the Defence and we would have no objection. It's video footage from a commercial television station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, we believe, Your Honour, it's Mr. Micic, this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just say thank you and noted, Your Honour, we'll look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the material is now available. We first leave it to the Defence. If finally the Chamber would -- if the Defence takes no action, if the Chamber would like to see it, then we'll let you know and then both parties have in their possession a copy. So then we move to item 10 on the agenda. That is about exemplars of contracts where the Chamber, as you may have noticed, wanted to find a little bit how widespread, how common it was. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think the issue in terms of its final resolution today might be a little premature. I say that for the following reasons. The information that I had available to me, I shared with the Defence. We were supposed to get back together again to discuss it. We have not had the occasion to do so. But let me in the meantime inform the Court what I have collected, and I have access to additional information and I seek the guidance of the Chamber in this respect. We have gone through our archival materials and we have copies of a number of municipal decisions regulating the departure of moving out of people from municipalities in the ARK region. I specifically referred to Kljuc, Petrovac, Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa, Prnjavor, Bosanski Novi, so we have the copy of the legislative framework from those decisions. Second of all we have very few exemplars of the type that gave rise to this issue, which was P340. We have some but we have very few. We -- much of that material, and -- that relates to that exhibit and similar types of decisions that were imposed on people leaving are found in witness statements. It's clear to me that our investigators didn't collect a great deal of that material; however, we do have access, I'm told, to that material. I'm told that my investigators have been in contact with the authorities in Bosnia and there are literally thousands of these types of reports. I have been forewarned from having my investigator go collect those until I find out approximately how many of those or what kind of guidance I can receive from the Trial Chamber in that respect. I'm told we can get access to those. So I'm at your disposal, Your Honours. I can provide you -- therefore I can provide with you a legislative framework materials, I can provide you with some limited number of exemplars, and I have access to other exemplars of the type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do they originate from several municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exemplars, how many municipalities would it cover?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have not received that information yet. What I have received is that there is an agency in Bosnia that has 3600 reports dealing with claims, property claims, approximately 70 per cent of those are dealing with housing issues. So I'm assuming based on this limited information that I have, those are the types of reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes. I can imagine that if you reclaim your property, that a file will be established, which perhaps not necessarily contains the document which was used once the property was abolished. So therefore, the Chamber, of course, has heard some evidence on the procedures established later to return and to claim again any property which is -- was lost or was supposed to be lost or by whatever means but the Chamber, of course, is specifically speaking for the documents signed or drafted at the moment when persons were leaving the municipality under circumstances which could at least raise the issue to what extent it was voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour as I say I have a very limited number of those exemplars and I could certainly ask my investigator to collect other exemplars from this agency that allegedly has them. I've not been in touch personally with that agency but I'm informed they have those types of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to give you the following guidance, Mr. Harmon. What the Chamber would like to see is examples of it and if that agency could, for example, say, this is a typical example of municipality X, we have 65 similar documents, but we give you one or two or three examples. If there are different types of documents, then we would like to receive copies of each of these types, and again, we would like to be informed how many of those documents are there. We don't have to see them all. Perhaps, of course, it is of importance if similar documents would be signed by all ethnicities, to be informed about that as well, whether it's a mono-ethnic enterprise or just Muslims or just Croats or just Serbs or just two or three of these groups. We would like to know that. We would like to know how many there would be available, and we would like to have a typical examples of those documents for the various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I've noted that. I'll proceed in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless, since the Chamber asked the Prosecution to engage in this effort, if there is any wish by the Defence to have this, to make it a bit wider, then, of course, please raise it so that we could invite the Prosecution to include that in their efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, such questions were going through our minds and rather a number of questions are raised by what Mr. Harmon has very fairly informed us all about this morning. Your Honour, we, with respect, would be content to proceed as Your Honour has just outlined to the Prosecution. The question then of whether any broadening needs to be done or where we go from there we suggest can be then faced at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if, of course, we could already see at this moment that for example if you'd like to know, I want the size of the property to be known as well, better ask it now so that we don't have to go into a second round, if you would consider that very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if anything had immediately struck us, to be added, we would have said so, and, Your Honour, it doesn't straight away so may we maybe leave it on that footing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that within the next 36 hours if something would come to your mind you would inform Mr. Harmon and he would be kind enough to include that in his request to his investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, there are two separate things, whether more or less immediately within the next day we think of things that we would like to be introduced straight away here in this exercise, then there still remains the question of when this first stage has been done, what then needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Your Honour we are perfectly content with that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's move to our next issue. The next issue on the agenda, under 11, is Prosecution wanted to make observations on the 65 ter summaries provided by the Defence. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I won't be long on this, Your Honour. Our observations on this point are what I have said on numerous occasions. There is a practice in this Court in respect of 65 ter summaries, they have to be factual, they have to be provided within a certain period of time, as do exhibits and we only reiterate our need to have that guidance complied with so we can properly organise our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd say I emphasise again that timing and quality is considered to be insufficient still at this moment, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The timing is certainly giving us some difficulties Your Honour, and given the manner in which we work, we need the time that is allotted by the guidance to complete our work properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may I, Mr. Stewart, especially if you would soon examine a witness which takes considerable time, take at the same time care that any 65 ter summaries for witnesses that would come after that would be provided in the accepted quality and within the time limits, and as early as possible to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we take on board both what Mr. Harmon has said and, of course, Your Honour's observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we move to item 12 on the agenda, which has been requested by the Defence, and that's the application of Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can deal with this extremely briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We want to say this: That the Defence have been in correspondence with the Prosecution on this issue. The Prosecution for the most part have answered most of the questions that we have hitherto raised. As a result of a lengthy letter from Mr. Harmon, we are going to respond to that in due course. I hope that the matter can be resolved between the parties but if not clearly we will have to bring it to the attention of the Court by way of motion. That's all I think I can usefully say this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you perhaps tell us whether your discussion is about 68 (i) or (ii)? Is it about exculpatory material or is it a wider, well, let's say the electronic disclosure which we find in the second paragraph of Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's basically in relation to exculpatory material. That's the area that the Defence are pursuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course that's always is a very sensitive issue also for the Chamber so the Chamber also hopes that the parties will resolve the matter. If not, of course, we'll hear from you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have now at item 14 on the agenda. We would like to clarify what the position is in relation to experts, because we -- two fields of expertise have been indicated by the Defence as fields in which they would like to produce expert reports. I think the Chamber did not find on the last list any experts, any more, which is perhaps not surprising because whether experts should be called or not depends on whether the other party accepts the report, yes or no, and whether they insist on cross-examination so I can imagine that you leave these experts out of the list because you assume that the other party would accept the report but it could also be that you don't want to present any expert reports, and especially since the Chamber I think said that the names should be disclosed to the other party already earlier this month, the Chamber is not aware of whether this has been done and whether there are still experts -- expert reports to be expected. Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, has item 13 been omitted for the same reason that sometimes football teams don't have a 13 player or airlines don't have a number 13 seat? Or are -- have we just missed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made a mistake in that respect, Mr. Stewart. I'm not that familiar with what happens on football teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the number 13, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that Johann Cruijff always had number 14. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As did [inaudible], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will deal with that after the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour the position is in fact quite different than anything Your Honour has supposed. It is bluntly this: In our assessment of our work and our examination of our work, and our consideration of what was required, particularly for counsel's work, let alone the support team, we faced -- well, have faced consistently but at the time when the question of responding and meeting directions in relation to expert evidence arose, we had such a massive deficit in terms of the time and hours available to do the work that required the hours it required, that we took one of the more robust decision that is we have been compelled to take in this case, and decided to cease any further exploration of the issue of expert evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we just struck them off the list. It's regrettable, Your Honour, because although -- I stand by what I indicated some weeks ago now, Your Honour, that this Defence team, acting on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf is not particularly wedded to the notion that excessive expert evidence is going to help anybody, but, Your Honour, we certainly would have preferred to reach a considered conclusion, but we haven't. Time is too short. Life is too short. We have been encouraged to take a robust approach. This is a far more robust approach than we would have wished, but we have adopted it. And that's the reason, Your Honour, they were deliberately taken off the list because there is frankly nothing we could do about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least that clarifies the issue, Mr. Stewart. I tend to agree with you that time is short. How long life will be, I don't know that yet but we will find that out as well. So we turn to 13, 92 bis witnesses. We find some 92 bis witnesses on the list. We also find some 92 bis witnesses on the list who have-- deceased. Could we hear from the Defence how they -- because we have not heard at this moment of any appointment of officers who would fulfil the formalities attached to the living 92 bis witnesses. We have not received any request on the admission of witnesses under 92 bis(D). So therefore the Chamber wonders what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we say it's a perfectly fair inquiry, Your Honour. If at some point we do put forward any 92 bis statement with an application for admission, then obviously that will be because we consider it important enough to do that. But in general, Your Honour, in relation to the not very many but few witnesses who have been identified on our list as candidates for 92 bis it is simply from our point of view no where near the top of the list of our priorities. We recognise that if we are going to make any application under 92 bis it's got to come at a time allowing it to be considered and in relation to those witnesses who are still alive obviously to consider the question of whether they may be asked to attend for cross-examination as a condition of admissibility but Your Honour that is the position. We are not -- we recognise that there comes a point at which it simply is in practice too late to make such an application but that's our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It came into my mind, Mr. Stewart, when I read that some witnesses under 92 bis were also 92 bis(D) witness as well, it will certainly not take any court time because cross-examination of witnesses who are deceased seems to be impossible so therefore it doesn't take any court time. It might add to the evidence you can present, present for the Defence case, so therefore we wondered, I mean, it's not a very complex matter. Of course, you have to look at the transcript of the -- or the statement given by the deceased witnesses but it's not a very complex matter to submit that to the Chamber. It doesn't take any court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour, as far as -- let's put it in those two categories. So far as the deceased witnesses are concerned cross-examination either doesn't apply or it's ineffective. The -- Your Honour, so far as those witnesses are concerned Your Honour is absolutely right. There is no more to be got from them obviously. But there may be, well, there is, perhaps a little bit of further background investigation that may require to be done but, Your Honour, I believe I can assure you that isn't going to be a problem. There is either going to be some 92 bis material from the deceased witnesses in the next week or so or there isn't. So far as the living witnesses are concerned, well, Your Honour is aware that that may not just potentially require more court time but the careful prepare significance of a 92 bis witness can take rather a lot of Defence team time, sometimes even more than viva voce witnesses to be confident that it can safely be put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We just draw the attention to this matter because if it's not five minutes to 12 then at least it's close to 12 if it's perhaps not ten minutes or quarter to 12 then we are approaching 12 o'clock. The Chamber is also interested to see that as much relevant evidence reaches the Chamber but, of course, at the same time the Chamber has set some time limits and so therefore you could consider this to be an encouragement, not to leave the Chamber without sources of information which might be relatively easily available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we'll accept it in that spirit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the next item, 15, on the agenda, unless the Defence would insist on open session, I would first go into private session because it might be an appropriate way of dealing with it, not necessarily but I leave it to the Defence and to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before Mr. Haider makes the call, in fact the Defence's position is that with just a small qualification, which we submit is not at all difficult, we would ask for it to be in public, open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The qualification is only this, Your Honour, that we would invite everybody and we have complete confidence in all those dealing with the matter to use discretion as to the precise treatment that Mr. Krajisnik is receiving which in fact is not detailed very much any way in the material before the Court. But Mr. Krajisnik otherwise is -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course a motion was filed confidentially and therefore the Chamber takes caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. Of course, it was our initiative to do that but Mr. Krajisnik, of course, is no more enthusiastic than any other human being to have such matters aired publicly. He is, after all, already here on trial for these charges in a public court so he would prefer it to be dealt with in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I leave it up to you, Mr. Stewart, in further arguing the matter to what extent you would give any further details. At this moment, I just mention that a confidential motion was filed and that as a result of that confidential motion, the Chamber has asked for some further medical information with the consent of the Accused to give this information to the Chamber, which is not exactly the same as this information to be filed and how to be filed but that's a matter perhaps you could raise at a later moment. I'll leave it to you at this moment to introduce the matter in this open session and add whatever you would like to add to your motion and also to pay attention to the reports we received yesterday, to the extent you deem that useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. While I'm introducing Your Honour, may I say I should have done it perhaps earlier but it's customary to introduce new members of our team. May I introduce Ms. Sarah Sheffield who is unhappily for us only temporarily but nevertheless very valuably assisting us in this case. If there were an Australian quota on the Defence team we are doing our best to keep it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, welcome in this courtroom, Ms. Sheffield. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- we -- of course, it's just today that we've had a chance to consider the reports and discuss them briefly with Mr. Krajisnik. The two reports without any -- no intended disparagement at all of the general practitioner attending to Mr. Krajisnik, the two reports are that they are largely one report because he for practical purposes says, well, yes, I endorse the -- and go along with the report received from the forensic psychiatrist who has sent him her report from Belgrade. Your Honour, our submission is that this report has certainly addressed specifically and helpfully the particular questions which Your Honour, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, framed and referred to the medical practitioners and it's a valuable and helpful step in resolving this matter. So far as the motion is concerned, what the report doesn't address, because in entire fairness it wasn't asked to address at this point, is particularly, if we look at paragraph 10 of our motion, C, the effect of his condition on ability to deal with the rigors of the case. Of course there are some implicit comments and some implicit guidance on these matters in the report but it's not a question specifically addressed. A, B, and D are for practical purposes quite closely addressed. So is E, present, prospective capability of working on his case. There is quite a lot of material in the report addressing that. It doesn't -- the reports were not asked to and therefore don't specifically address F, which is really critically important and also it ties in, of course, with the whole scheduling question, G, the prospect, desirability, and ability of Mr. Krajisnik to give evidence for, well, what is normally contemplated, about four hours a day, five days a week, for what on everybody's expectation would be a period of at least five consecutive weeks. Well, that's certainly the expectation as it stood when the motion was filed.
