So, Your Honour, we do welcome this report as a first step, but we do then, in the light of this report, which is positive, of course, in relation to the effects of the treatment, that it's clear that happily the treatment has been having some clear, beneficial effect and, Your Honour, it wouldn't be out of place here, without usurping anybody's function, to acknowledge that that is consistent with the Defence team's own observations, because we have thought it our responsibility and we did some considerable time ago alert the Registry to such observations as we were clearly able to make and certainly Your Honour that is consistent with our own observations over the very recent past. But, Your Honour, we nevertheless submit that the matter is of sufficient importance and significance that this most helpful report from Dr. Petrovic should be regarded now as justifying and requiring a further specific examination rather than a retrospective report of examinations already conducted, which addresses the precise matters in the motion and brings the matter right up to date. Your Honour, we, so far as the identity of the person conducting the report is concerned, we would have absolutely no difficulty whatever with it being a further examination and report by Dr. Petrovic, as soon as that can conveniently be arranged. That would seem in many ways to be absolutely the most practical and helpful thing to do rather than chopping and changing from one person to another. But we do suggest that this retrospective report of relatively brief examinations and we don't think that there is any special contest about that although it is a very helpful report, should lead on to the full examination which we do request in the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Harmon, perhaps before I give an opportunity to you, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Krajisnik, is there anything you would like to add to what Mr. Stewart just raised? Because, of course, this is a matter on which not the knowledge of the law or even the knowledge of the facts is of vital importance but, of course, you're the one who is best able to add whatever you think it is you want to add.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very unwilling to discuss this subject, but I think that Mr. Stewart, basically, said everything that matters. I had come to the very end, to so speak, and that is why I sought the assistance of the doctors and they really helped me in a comprehensive manner. The situation is better now. Not everything has been resolved though. There are many things that need to be done in addition to what has already been done in order to bring this to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say many things have been done which need to be done but there are still other things to be done to bring this to an end, do you -- do you refer to medical attention? Perhaps psychological, psychiatric attention to be paid to your present condition, or were you referring to what happens in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, so far as it's the latter, perhaps the -- with respect, Mr. Krajisnik's participation at this point could be confined to the former because the latter is another item on the agenda, connected, of course, in various obvious ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if Mr. Krajisnik speaks a sentence, at least I would like to know -- I'm not asking him to elaborate on it but I just wanted to be sure that I understood his last portion of his observation rightly. That means whether he was referring to mainly medical condition and what has to be done in that area or whether he, with that sentence, also referred to what happens in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, what I had in mind was that the situation, the way I understand it, as a lay person, and that contributed to my condition, is the fact that for over two years I slept in storage, basically, and now some measures have been taken, will contribute to making the premises more fitting. I believe the doctors on the other hand are fair and that they will do the right things. I find this embarrassing but I have to say that as I lived in this storage room among these archives, I would sweat six times during the night. Now I sweat only twice. So I don't have to get up all the time to change. I believe that would be sufficient. The doctors are going to take measures. I know what the situation is like. The doctors will deal with it professionally. I need these archives so I need these things, but then I agree with what Mr. Stewart said as well, as for the rest. So that is basically what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to give an opportunity to Mr. Harmon to respond to the motion. Please be seated. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have very little to say about this motion. We reviewed the reports that we received today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I may interrupt you, Mr. Harmon. I should have put on the record that apart from the medical information we received, that we also received information about some developments in the, well, let's say, the housing of Mr. Krajisnik and the housing of his files. I take it that the parties got copies of that information in exactly the same form as we received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have very little to say about this motion, Your Honour. Our principal concern is that we proceed with this case in a proper fashion, and that we proceed as quickly as is desirable on this case. I have just reviewed this report. I have looked at counsel's motions, under F and G, those points specifically do not appear to be addressed in the report. I think that if there is -- if the Court is inclined to have the doctors revisit these two issues, our only concern is that it be done very, very quickly, obviously within the framework of a proper forensic examination but it be done very quickly. Those are our only submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber considers it wiser at this moment to first take some time for reflection. Whether that would still be today or tomorrow is another matter. But we want to exchange our views in order to form the opinion of the Chamber on whether your request for a further psychiatric examination, as you said, what was there is the first step, whether that's really the first step or the last step, we'll consider that, and give as soon as possible a decision on it. And it's clear that you said that F and G were not -- and C were not specifically included, and I emphasise specifically included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, may I emphasise Your Honour that while we recognise that a number of these elements in paragraph 10 of the motion have, as I said, by implication been at least partly covered, Your Honour, we do certainly adhere to our submission that it isn't just a question of specifically. Those points are not covered in the report in any substantial way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we move on to the next item on the agenda. No, there is one issue which needs some attention, and I again address Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, you gave your consent for the Chamber to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can answer this, Your Honour, because I have discussed it specifically with Mr. Krajisnik. It was understood and is confirmed, if there is any doubt, that the consent extended to anybody in the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, in the registry, and, of course, Mr. Krajisnik's own defence team having free access to these medical reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That it would mean that filing, but confidential filing would then be appropriate for these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we suggest that it would. That such information as has inevitably been revealed in this public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber instructs the Registry to -- would that -- I take it -- just include the medical reports and not the report on new storage facilities? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- we suggest that the filing cabinets at this institution don't need to be cluttered up with further copies about stuff about filing cabinets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would seem to fill the filing cabinets on reports on cabinets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It could go on forever, couldn't it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the Registrar is instructed to file confidentially the reports made by Mr. Falke dated the 21st of February 2006 and the report by Dr. Vera Petrovic, a neuropsychiatrist, dated the 18th of February 2006. Filing should take place confidentially. Yes, that's what I said already. Then we come to our final -- the last point on the agenda which is scheduling of Defence witnesses and practical matters related to the accused's testimony. Perhaps just for the record there has been a request by the Defence to delay the beginning of the testimony to be given by Mr. Krajisnik until next Wednesday, the 1st of March. The Chamber has denied that request, but at the same time has moved the next Monday, that's the 27th of February, hearing to the afternoon, giving in this way, at least an opportunity to -- for some communication between Defence counsel and the Accused before the testimony would start. Then the Chamber has received an information that the Defence had decided to call two witnesses to give testimony first, starting on the 27th of February, and the Chamber has then decided the parties are informed about that, that this rescheduling of the -- well, that was not -- the information the parties received is that the Chamber decided that the victims and witnesses section should not take any further action at this moment on getting these witnesses in The Hague, for the apparent reason that the Chamber expected Mr. Krajisnik to be the next witness to be examined and that such a change in the programme would at least have needed the prior consent of the Chamber. I take it, Mr. Stewart, that the issue is primarily of importance to you, although, of course, it's also important for the Prosecution and the Chamber so I would like to give you an opportunity first to submit whatever you would like to submit in this respect to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue is of absolutely central importance to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I said but most of all for you, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes and no, in a sense. It is, of course, it's -- for Mr. Krajisnik, when you say you mean Mr. Krajisnik, in effect, and us representing them. I understand that, Your Honour. Yes, of course, for Mr. Krajisnik it's most important of all because he's the man on trial but it is of central importance to everybody, by which I mean everybody beyond this court, that this matter is approached with the utmost care and conscientious by all concerned. The position is this: Mr. Krajisnik wishes to give evidence in his own defence. That has been his unequivocal position since -- well, as far as I recall, the beginning, very beginning of the trial. It's been reiterated on a number of occasions. I don't believe that there has ever been any suggestion or contradiction of that emanating from the Defence or Mr. Krajisnik included in that definition, of course. He quite naturally wishes to give evidence when he is and feels adequately prepared to do that. And unsurprisingly, that position is 100 per cent endorsed and supported, as it must be, by his counsel and the rest of his Defence team. I professionally, on this -- I have the overall conduct of the case on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf. Many decisions are decisions which are for me to take after appropriate consultation with Mr. Krajisnik. The decision whether Mr. Krajisnik gives evidence or not is his, and I naturally, loyally implement that decision, and I've indicated again clearly to Your Honour on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik, which way in principal that decision goes. Nevertheless it is my professional responsibility to Mr. Krajisnik, and as a matter of fact, to the Court, and all concerned, not to take the initiative to put Mr. Krajisnik in the witness box at a point where he is not in, I'll say "our" because the team of two counsel presenting this case, not in our professional judgement, ready and adequately prepared to do himself justice by his own evidence. And that, in exactly the same way that we loyally and professionally give 100 per cent support to Mr. Krajisnik's decision whether or not to give evidence, he gives and has indicated to us, 100 per cent support for our professional judgement on that particular matter. Your Honour, it is our professional judgement that Mr. Krajisnik is not near ready. We, as a team, I'll put it that way, because it is -- there is no difference, there is no point in drawing -- no value in drawing any division or distinction, we are Mr. Krajisnik for these purposes. We work with him. We are a team. Mr. Krajisnik is the central person in that team. We, as a team, are not adequately prepared to put Mr. Krajisnik in the witness box in the confidence that he is anywhere near ready to do himself justice. Therefore, Your Honour, we cannot do that. The -- we wish to achieve that as soon as we can. It is apparent, whatever else happens at the next stage, but it is apparent that the matters which have been dealt with in the report under the previous item in the agenda, will not have made that task any easier. In fact, it's blindingly obvious that they will have made it harder. But that isn't the key. They have made, of course, harder what was already a hard and, in practice, impossible task, to meet the target and constantly moving target. The 1st of February date almost put forward in desperation, Your Honour, but then anxiously reconsidered, with our coming to the conclusion which I have just summarised for Your Honours. So Your Honour may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 1st of February, you're referring to, there was a question of delaying, making the 27th of February the -- what we understood to be the 1st of March but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have constantly slipped. I'm afraid that I made a slip in -- I made that slip in writing and it's embedded in my head. I'll try to disembed it. The 1st of March, absolutely right, Your Honour, thank you. Yes, the 1st -- everything I said applies mutatis mutandis the 1st of March. We gave it, and we is all of us, anxious consideration and have come to the conclusion which I have just summarised for Your Honours. In the -- in that light, having felt the absolute need a few weeks ago, I forget exactly when, to stop the relentless flow of defence witnesses, with the massive call that that makes, massive drain it makes all the time on the resources of this small Defence team, we felt the need to stop that flow and work on Mr. Krajisnik's evidence, with all the difficulties inherent in the current situation. We recognised that the Court had directed to the case should -- well, must, it was what the Court was ordering -- evidence should restart on the 27th. The Court order strictly speaking did not include a direction or order that it should restart with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We checked that carefully, Mr. Stewart. The Chamber was informed that the next witness that would be called would be Mr. Krajisnik, and on that basis the Chamber did not need it necessary to include the name of Mr. Krajisnik in that because the Chamber would expect the Defence to indicate any change of order before it would decide that -- at least to approach the Chamber before changing the order which was so clearly focusing on Mr. Krajisnik to be the next witness. That has been said again and again and again. So therefore the Chamber felt no need to expressly make that a part of its order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I note that, Your Honour. We read and did read the order, but that's -- Your Honour, that's the way -- whatever the underlying reasons and thinking, the way the order is expressed is, I do submit, as I have just summarised it. But, Your Honour, perhaps we should just move on any way, with respect. We, based on whatever understanding we had, we understood the Court was ordering that evidence should resume on the 27th. So not being remotely ready, properly, to put Mr. Krajisnik in the witness box, the only way we could comply with that was by bringing urgently other witnesses. And that is what we did. And that is what we arranged. And we arranged witnesses who are from within the group, that we have notified to both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution recently as our -- if you like, our priority list for the immediate future. And so we did arrange that. And, well, Your Honour knows the position was the Court wished those arrangements to be unscrambled. The Prosecution agreed with the Trial Chamber that those arrangements should be unscrambled. I was specifically asked the other morning whether I would agree to the immediate unscrambling of the arrangements to which we had given such careful consideration and urgent attention on the Defence side. Not surprisingly, I did not agree. And that was where we were. But within a very short time the Court made that direction any way and effectively overrode our arrangements and told the Victims and Witnesses Unit not to bring the witnesses we had arranged to bring. Your Honour, may we simply observe we don't fully, with respect, see why that was necessary, given that there would have been ample time to call those witnesses after this morning's hearing any way. They weren't travelling for another couple of days, and Your Honour, we have no wish to cause unnecessary inconvenience to any witness on the Defence side and hope that we haven't done that. But Your Honour, any way, be that as it may, we are now in the position where the Trial Chamber has called off those witnesses for next week. We do not have witnesses for next week. Your Honour, we are not on the Defence side, professionally and responsibly willing to subject Mr. Krajisnik to evidence at this point. We regard it as a breach of our professional duty to do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What were the preparation is insufficient? You'll understand, Mr. Stewart, that the claim was quite surprised that -- I think it's only two weeks ago that you said that the 27th would not be the right date but two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I tried to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You said you did it in a desperate mood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can explain it more fully. Your Honour encouraged me to be brief about such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you -- I asked you whether -- I said, as a matter of fact, that you would understand that we were a bit surprised by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That I do understand, Your Honour, yes, I acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now to hear that Mr. Krajisnik is not near or that the Defence is not near to be ready, it's not entirely clear to me. I take it that a witness testifies on the basis of his recollection of facts about which he is asked. I also take it that Defence counsel need to discuss and to study what are the relevant areas on which evidence should be given. It's not entirely clear to me at this moment whether the Defence counsel are not sufficiently prepared to formulate questions or whether there is any other reason why the Defence, which is counsel and the Accused, would not be ready after two years of hearing this case now to tell us what is relevant for us to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm afraid I can't do that right now because if Your Honour really wants the full account of the reasons and the background and why over two years we have got to this point, that is, A, going to take a very long time, and, B, is more suitably the subject of a formal application by the Defence. But, Your Honour, the -- may -- let's be realistic, please, may we, I ask rhetorically. This Trial Chamber has imposed, for a very long time, a deadline or date on the Defence, which has been extended, I forget precisely when it was extended sometime around November, last November, extended by seven weeks, so that's how we got to the 28th of April, so since before the new year, the 28th of April has been the date. The Defence was, and I'm talking about before that notification to the Trial Chamber of the 1st of March, that it remains the position, in effect, the Defence is faced with this. We have a client who wishes fervently, to give evidence in his own defence before the Defence case closes. We have a client whose evidence does, despite what Your Honour has just said, require the most careful and thorough and detailed preparation, and apart from anything else it requires such preparation if it's going to be given remotely efficiently within the time that anybody would hope it to be presented in. We have then to work back, unless and until that date is changed, we have to work back from the date of the 28th of April, to try to allow for adequate time to present Mr. Krajisnik's evidence-in-chief, and it's perfectly clear under the rules that is our job and that's what we do. Of course, to make allowance for Judges' questions that may come from time to time along the way or at the end of examination by counsel and the application we do and can only assume for the purposes of all our assessment and calculation of the 60 per cent guideline about which the Trial Chamber has tended to become firm, for cross-examination by the Prosecution. In addition to that, we have to accommodate the reasonable need, and I should add the very strong wish, of Mr. Krajisnik that a number of other witnesses on our list should come and give evidence in his support. Also, of course, trying to keep in mind the necessity to review in the light of Mr. Krajisnik's own evidence what are then the top priorities in terms of that other evidence. This task, given the number of witnesses remaining on the very reduced Defence list, is an extremely daunting task. But central to that task remains the essential point that it is not right, it is not fair, we do not do our proper duty as Mr. Krajisnik's counsel if we take the initiative ourselves to put him in the witness box when in our judgement he's not ready. I'm repeating myself now, Your Honour, but that is the position. So we wished then, noting the Court's order that we should restart, we wished to use those days. We wished to call some of that other evidence that Mr. Krajisnik and we, for that matter, on his behalf, Mr. Krajisnik wishes to be called on his behalf. But, Your Honour, exploration of the reasons why we are not ready -- well, Your Honour, if the Trial Chamber does wish to conduct a full investigation and inquiry into that matter, well, with respect it should do it. And it should look at every aspect of the history of this case and it should look at everything that has led up to this point, and not be selective about it. Your Honour, one thing I should say frankly is that the Defence has already decided that it cannot live with the deadline of the 28th of April. Your Honour, we will abide by court orders. This is not a -- this is not a civil disobedience, Your Honour. We are responsible counsel. In the end, what is ordered by this Court, we will do, and if those orders are unscrambled by the Appeals Chamber at any point, we will do whatever the Appeals Chamber orders we should do. It doesn't mean, though, Your Honour, that we are not going to firmly take whatever steps in our professional judgement we consider are proper to take on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf when in our judgement the position does not allow us and him adequately to present his defence. That is our judgement, Your Honour. Your Honours make the ultimate subject, the Appeals Chamber's make the ultimate judgements in the legal framework on these matters. We make our professional judgement about what steps to take, and, Your Honour, that is about as clearly and fairly as we can manage to put it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, let me just see whether I and the Chamber understood you well. What you're saying is the Defence is not ready to call Mr. Krajisnik at this moment. When Mr. Krajisnik wants to testify in his own case, when he will be ready, we'll learn that somewhere in the future, we'll abide by your orders, but we know already that we are not in a position to finish the case by the 28th of April, and if you order, as you did until now, that Mr. Krajisnik would start his testimony next Monday, we'll strike him from the list? Is that a correct understanding? Because we consider him not to be ready, it's our responsibility, and despite the fact that you indicated in the beginning that you would call him, which is, I think, fully in accordance with the tradition you come from, we would call him as the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's too late for that, Your Honour, isn't it? With respect. That point has gone a very long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you really, Mr. Stewart, when I refer to this, want to explain to me that he could not be called any more as the first witness? Mr. Stewart, do you really think that this Chamber would not understand that without your comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've envisioned the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Stewart, I want you first now to listen. I was speaking. I was referring to your tradition, in which the Accused testifies first, and then you considered it necessary to interrupt me to tell the Chamber that calling Mr. Krajisnik as the first witness was not possible any more. You should have refrained from doing that, and I'll continue where I was. I was asking myself -- I was pointing -- putting it to you whether we did understand the Defence's position well, despite the fact that you indicated, in the very beginning, that you would call him as the first witness, which, as far as this Chamber understands, but if I'm wrong, you may respond to that at a later stage, that is in accordance with the tradition you come from, and that later on, the moment on which Mr. Krajisnik would testify has been delayed several times, I didn't learn them by heart but I remember there was after the Christmas recess several dates in February were mentioned or late January, then the proposal was let's delay it from the 27th of February until the 1st of March, and now your latest announcement is "we are not ready and when we will be ready it's something we do not know yet, and if we feel that we are not ready, we cannot possibly call Mr. Krajisnik to the stand," which at first I would be understood, that is if the Chamber would insist on continuing this trial next Monday and would insist on Mr. Krajisnik to be the next witness, that you would strike him from the list? That's a question, whether that's a correct understanding. I'm just verifying whether we understood your position well. You may comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I first of all -- may I apologise if I was abrupt and hasty and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apology accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- in interrupting Your Honour? May I also explain with respect, though, that my comment was with respect a little bit more subtle than Your Honour seems to believe. I was not being so insolent as simply to point out to the Trial Chamber that somebody who hadn't been called as the first witness could no longer be called as the first witness. With respect, Your Honour, I wouldn't insult Your Honour's intelligence or my own for that matter with such an observation. The point about it was this, Your Honour: That once the opportunity has been lost of Mr. Krajisnik being the first witness, with advantages to his case as well, because that means that, as I would understand it, is one of the reasons for this convention, that then because the accused has to be in court to hear the other witnesses, he then gives his evidence before hearing those other witnesses and can, in effect, submit, well, I gave my evidence clean, as it were, without seeing those other witnesses, once that advantage has been lost so that we have -- and once the advantage of being able to review what other witnesses come along in the light of his evidence, it's really pretty marginal then whether he comes as witness number 16, witness number 18, witness number 19. That was my only point there, Your Honour, that it's water under the bridge there, so Your Honour's reference to our wishing to call him first, which would have been our earnest wish, we are now in a position where, of course, that can't be done but the same considerations simply don't arise. Now, we are faced with overwhelming different considerations which are far more important. May I also say that some of the ways in which Your Honour then seeks to summarise and then paraphrase what I've said make what I've said, with respect, sound rather more dismissive and rather more cavalier than they are intended to be. In fact they are not intended to be cavalier or dismissive at all. They are intended to be carefully considered. What the Defence -- the -- the one thing the Trial Chamber cannot do, with respect, it cannot tell Mr. Krajisnik to go into the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Krajisnik, it's his own choice whether he wants to remain silent or whether he want to testify in his own case that's without any question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The order of presenting evidence, however, is under the direction of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's -- Your Honour has really upped the ante in effect because Your Honour is directly questioning me on this and seeing where we go and you're saying, well, if, as I understand it, and I hesitate if I'm inaccurately paraphrasing or representing what Your Honour says, then of course I stand to be immediately corrected. Your Honour is saying, what if we the Trial Chamber tell you, having called off these other witnesses, what -- we tell you that if you must call Mr. Krajisnik, if you're going to call him at all, you must call him next Monday, and Your Honour is supposing we then have the choice, do we call him next Monday or are we compelled to strike him off the list. There are other options, Your Honour. We can say, no, I'm afraid we cannot call Mr. Krajisnik because he isn't ready. In our judgement, he isn't ready, it is not safe to put him in the witness box, then we have to apply, formally, properly, and comprehensively for whatever extensions are necessary for Mr. Krajisnik's case to be properly presented, thoroughly presented, an adequate number of witnesses to be called and for Mr. Krajisnik to be fitted it properly in that programme. Your Honour, that is what we will do. Your Honour, it goes beyond Mr. Krajisnik's evidence. It is perfectly clear in our submission that this -- and I'm not making the application today, Your Honour, because I'm not going, with respect, I'm not going to be put in a position of having to make an application in about two sentences which the Court can then brush aside. This application, as and when an application or an extension is made is going to have to be done properly because we have seen what happens if applications are not done thoroughly and if the opportunity is given for the matter not to be thoroughly and completely considered. Your Honour, this timetable, we have -- one thing we have been absolutely consistent about, we have said that this timetable will not work. Your Honour, I did tell the Court, and that's also true, that we have made our plans and we have worked to try to make it work. We have done that. We have not made our plans, done our scheduling, we've not done it on some blythe assumption that we could ignore the date of the 28th of April. We have absolutely -- that's why, in the end, and I say desperation, it's why we were driven to just try to put forward this date. We know how much Mr. Krajisnik wants to give evidence in his own case. How on earth are we going to fit that in is the problem we've been facing. How on earth are we going to fit that in with other witnesses? The position is we really can't as things stand, and Your Honour, with respect, Your Honour, we do question, how in the circumstances the Court feels that it could even contemplate the sort of procedure which Your Honour has just alluded to, without fully considering and resolving the issue under item 14 in the agenda on which the Court -- 15, I beg your pardon, on which Your Honour has made it expressly clear that the Trial Chamber has not reached a decision, and Your Honours need to discuss it among yourselves. We, with respect, don't clearly understand and see how those matters fit together. But, Your Honour, you can -- you can question how it is that after two years Mr. Krajisnik is not ready to give evidence. All I can tell you, I can't tell you in a sentence as a fact, Your Honour, all I can tell you is in our professional judgement is, he is no where near. And whatever the reasons. If in the end you want to say it's money, it's incompetence, it's laziness, it's idleness, it is disorganisation, it's whatever it is, it is possible that it is the impossible schedule imposed by this Court and those involved with this Court in determining what scheduling apply to these cases. It is possible, Your Honour, and we are likely very soon urgently to require this with respect to ask this Trial Chamber to consider that as the real cause of the difficulty we are in. And I started by saying it goes far beyond Mr. Krajisnik because if Mr. Krajisnik's case is not done properly, if he's not able to give his evidence fairly when he's ready to give it, if he doesn't therefore receive a fair Defence, then what is this institution here for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stewart, allow me to ask you a rather pragmatic question, of a very practical nature. When you say that you aren't ready, or that your client, Mr. Krajisnik, is not ready to give evidence, is -- when you state this, I feel rather concerned. When is one actually ready? At what point in time do you think he will be ready? Can you leave the Bench hanging in the air like that? How long will it take? Six months? One year? Two years? Do you understand that we would like to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can understand that very well. We would like to know as well, and always would have done. It's a very anxious question for us. Your Honour's question is entirely fair. I don't reject it as an entirely fair question. Your Honours will forgive me if I always show a certain nervousness about giving estimates and dates, just based on the concern that they are understood to be what they are, that they are estimates and that we struggle to know ourselves. Your Honour, the question familiar to every lawyer, when is one actually ready, a bit like doing an exam, you're never ready in the sense that would you'd always like to have more time somewhere. Your Honour, we are -- between us, these counsel, we do have rather a lot of experience. We are familiar with that question. We are familiar with that feeling. It is a matter of professional judgement. You'll never be perfectly ready. We have indicated this morning the type of robust decision which this Defence team is willing and able to take, and more robust, we submit, than a lot of lawyers might feel comfortable with, and we have made many very robust decisions along the way in relation to this case. But so far as this is concerned, it is a matter of judgement. Your Honours, we are not going to -- we assure you this much -- we are not going to err on the side of some sort of excessive wish to cover all bases of some sort of perfectionism. No client likes to hear his lawyers say they are not perfectionists but Mr. Krajisnik will understand if we acknowledge that some realistic balance has to be adopted. We are not going to adopt that approach. But we are -- we simply know, as a matter of professional judgement, we simply know that we are not at that point. It's -- you can't define an elephant as easily as you can recognise it and we can recognise that. So that's the position. So far as estimates are concerned, if we are remaining, and at the moment the cutoff date is the 28th of April, if we are able to do nothing whatever about that, in the sense that after we had gone through all procedurals and we don't want to waste time on that but I'm sure Your Honours will also understand that any application of that nature also takes enormous amount of time away from the other task and that is a real, real practical problem but if we end up, as a matter of judgement and if they are involved, the Appeals Chamber, if we end up with the 28th of the April as the end of the Defence case, then I will be frank, Mr. Krajisnik does wish to give evidence. But we are not going to call him on the 27th of April to give ludicrous evidence for four hours and then say, well, the Prosecution is has two hours, 40 minutes, or whatever it is, it's not exactly that, it's 2.4 hours or something. We're not going to say that, tempting but we are not going to do it. On the other hand there may very well be an assessment on our part of the balance from our point of view of when we are properly ready to call Mr. Krajisnik to give evidence and what ground we can cover, how much time we can cover, always bearing in mind that it is true that more preparation time we take the more efficiently we can shorten the examination-in-chief, and I do assure Your Honour that very serious practical steps have been taken, are continuing to be taken, in the -- what we aim to be with all the difficulties, as streamlined an approach to evidence as we can manage with certainly serious use of such electronic means as are available to stop paper being distributed all over the Court in a wasteful way. So we are working on it, Your Honour. I can say in answer to His Honour Judge Hanoteau's question, we are not saying six months, we wouldn't mind six months, we've seen how massively this case can expand, even things we've referred to this morning in relation to these reports on movements of population indicate how much this case has of serious stuff which is still not within the vast quantity of material before the Court. But, Your Honour, what we wish to do is we wish to make our own, in the -- what in a sense the normal way. We wish to make our own professional judgements about which witnesses we call and when we call them, in Mr. Krajisnik's interests, if the case is to finish on the 28th of April then it will finish on the 28th of April. If we make an application and if Your Honours do see that in the interests of justice there ought to be an extension, well, that will give us the opportunity, no doubt, to cover Mr. Krajisnik's own evidence thoroughly and to call more of the still-material and relevant witnesses who are on our reduced witness list. But, Your Honour, we are not in a -- we are not in a mode of blatant non-cooperation in relation to this. We just want Mr. Krajisnik to be able to do himself justice when he gives his evidence. It's really no more and no less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg of you not to mention the date of the 28th of April. Please, do not mention the date of the 28th of April. I would just like to ask you to answer this question: When can you start with the examination of Mr. Krajisnik? Just like that. Because you said you needed some time to prepare his examination, as you call it. When will you be ready? When can you start? We should not mention any other dates or anything else. When can you actually start? Is this a clear question? If you can't answer, don't answer. I'm just putting this question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can answer. Mr. Krajisnik has a view. I have a view. Mr. Josse has a view which on last talking was not significantly different from my own. But -- well, I -- I will answer Your Honour's question but may I have a short while to discuss it, up to date, with Mr. Josse and Mr. Krajisnik, and any other member of my team, because my support team come into this in a serious way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it's surprising that you need to consult at this moment on this very question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, not really, with respect, Your Honour, because it's -- I'm being asked -- I know what I'm being asked. I am being asked something that you will hold me to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's surprising to us. Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I comment, Your Honour, on that because I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stewart. Please take your time to do what you said you would need to do? Would we have to withdraw for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not something I can really conveniently discuss with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Josse in the corner of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then. How much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 15 minutes, Your Honour, please. I see the time. Well, it's 25 past 1.00. Well, ten minutes, if we go straight through to see Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've got your ten minutes, Mr. Stewart. We will adjourn until 25 minutes to two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I am aware that our generosity is not always very impressive in your mind but after these 12 minutes could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll take two minutes wherever I can get them Your Honour, thank you. It's Judge Hanoteau's question but I'm quite sure it effectively comes from the entire Trial Chamber. Your Honour, we had a four-person discussion with Mr. Karganovic our case manager who is an interpreter. Your Honour, if we -- we would have to make one or two assumptions. If we assume that there is no significant problem arising out of the issue under number 15 on the agenda, we have to make an assumption, if we assume that we do not continue with other witnesses, so that we are, apart from absolutely essential other tasks, we are working on preparing Mr. Krajisnik's evidence, then, with also these assurances, Your Honour, the answer to Your Honour's question is not grossed up for negotiating purposes, it has absolutely no fat built into it by comparison with the genuine opinions of the people concerned, if we start with Mr. Krajisnik's view, just for purposes of presentation. Mr. Krajisnik's own personal view is that we cannot be adequately ready for his evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Cannot be adequately ready to begin his evidence until the 1st of May. That coincided, not endorsed by, for practical purposes within a day really exactly coincided with the view of one of the counsel, and was barely significantly different from the view of the other counsel. I don't believe it would be necessary or appropriate then to go into further detail about those internal discussions but that is the position, Your Honour. We -- that's the -- Your Honour asked us. We take the question in the spirit of absolutely genuine inquiry and we accept Your Honour's invitation to put the 28th of April for the purposes of answering this question absolutely on one side. That's the answer, Your Honour. I hope and trust that that is helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has indicated that Mr. Krajisnik wishes to give evidence when he feels he is adequately prepared to give evidence. Has there been sufficient time for him to get adequately prepared to give evidence? It's our submission, Your Honour, that the test is an objective test and the factors that I would point to Your Honour's consideration in assessing this test are the following: There has been a lengthy and costly investigation pre-trial, before the opportunity for Mr. Stewart to take the case, presumably Mr. Krajisnik studied the results carefully of that investigation. The second factor is he has sat through this case for two years. He has received copies of all of the Prosecution exhibits and he has at his disposal, as we know, a considerable archives that he's had an opportunity over two years, since the commencement of this case and frankly before, to review to prepare himself for this case. He has had the indictment for a considerable period of time, so he knows the type of a case to meet, and he's had our pre-trial brief so he knows what type of days he has to meet. Three, he has had many breaks specifically designed for preparing for his evidence. There have been gaps of weeks so he can prepare for his evidence. Those are the objective factors that we submit, Your Honour, should be considered, and the test for us is an objective test. Has there been sufficient time for him to objectively -- adequately prepare to give evidence? Our answer to that question is yes, based on the objective criteria that I've set forth. I want to put aside obviously the medical issue that has arisen that we've discussed but the objective assessment in our view is there has been sufficient time for Mr. Krajisnik to be adequately prepared to take the witness stand and to give evidence. Those are our submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, any need to respond to what Mr. Harmon said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In a sense, Your Honour, Mr. Harmon is giving a summarised version of an answer to an application that we haven't yet made. Your Honour, that's my only comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we close this session, if Mr. Krajisnik, who has at various occasions told us that he would like to be actively involved in his defence, and his the different positions, although almost the same, have been presented to us, including the one of Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to give an opportunity to Mr. Krajisnik to add, if there is anything he would like to add, what has been said until now. Mr. Krajisnik. I'm not urging you to do so but I'm just giving you the opportunity to add anything you would like to add.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have heard what Mr. Stewart had to say. We had an objective conversation about the best way to approach my testimony. I'm afraid that there might have been a mistake that might have slipped in due to language problems, because both the lawyer and the Accused must prepare accordingly and you yourselves are aware of that. That's all I have to add. And I fully support my Defence team and I'm very grateful for the fact that they summoned up the courage to say, as they have said, that my Defence would not be adequate at this stage for a whole range of reasons that I wouldn't like to elaborate on at the moment because I'm afraid it might be redundant. Thank you very much for your attention and I do agree with the Defence team. There is something else, I apologise, there maybe a point which may have been skipped or something, something that should have been on the agenda. I think it was item 15 and I'm extremely grateful for the fact that it figures on the agenda in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have not dealt with the second portion of agenda item 15 or 16? No, let me just -- you said 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's good that you remind us. We expressly wanted to give you an opportunity. We would rather do that once we finish 16 and then go back to that specific part of 15. Mr. Stewart, I have a similar short question. To the extent possible, could you please give as short an answer as possible. Judge Hanoteau has asked you about the day when you would expect the Defence to be ready to call Mr. Krajisnik as a witness in his own case. Until now, we have been provided with a number of 175 hours and then later on we had different numbers, less than 70 or more than 70, or -- and you may have noticed that the Chamber in its scheduling order used different figures. What is the present position of the Defence in that respect? And, of course, I'm asking you for an estimate again or that you say that you stick to the 175 and don't be afraid to become nervous if you have to give estimates because the Chamber becomes just as nervous if -- when it hears your estimates. So please, could you please tell us whether we are still at the 175 or at 70 or at -- or whether you would accept the time scheduled by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are still around 175, unable to see a concrete basis for a significant change, but I would say this, Your Honour: The overwhelming likelihood is that we will be able to reduce that estimate rather than increase it on this basis. That's -- I'm really confident that with adequate preparation time we would be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That practically would mean that in your position, let's just assume that you would start -- given all the other matters you would start on the 1st of May, then for 175 hours, and let me take it very optimistically that would bring us examination-in-chief only until the end of June, and then it would take us another five weeks for cross-examination, and perhaps the Chamber might have a few questions for Mr. Krajisnik as well. That brings us well into December -- in September, far into September, and then one of the conditions was that we would not -- that no other testimony would be heard before Mr. Krajisnik starts. Then let's just assume that there would be another 10, 20 witnesses, let's take it very optimistically again, each witness four hours, which is below the average, cross-examination, well, all together another 60, 70 hours, well, let's say another four weeks so half October, then the question becomes whether the Chamber would be in a position to deliver judgement before Christmas. Is that a realistic approach as I present it to you now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does flow from my realistic answer to Judge Hanoteau's realistic question. These consequences would appear to flow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear and short. The next issue, then, unless there is anyone who would like to raise anything under the heading of 16 again, I think the Chamber in one of the messages to the parties explained that it would like to hear, if Mr. Krajisnik considers that relevant to him or about his concerns about his concerns about the French case. I immediately add to that that this Chamber, of course, has no competence in any way to interfere with a domestic jurisdiction in civil matters, but nevertheless, since it was raised as a matter of concern which was at the basis of the confidential motion, of course, the Chamber would like to know if there is anything, any update that would make us better understand the causes of the concerns of Mr. Krajisnik. We would like to hear from him. I don't know whether it's you, Mr. Krajisnik, you are yes, you reminded me that it's -- it was still on the agenda. So whether it's you or counsel who will inform us, I leave that up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it is Mr. Krajisnik on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be any need to go into private session for the matter then -- I mean, it's -- we are now in open session and I don't know whether the other parties in the civil procedure are listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I should think, Your Honour, that we would start with Mr. Krajisnik just having very clearly in mind that we are in public so that if at any point he felt that there was something he wanted to say which shouldn't be public, he would be alert to mention that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Krajisnik should be aware that among the public may be the claimants in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honour is in effect warning to Mr. Krajisnik that he should take great care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That he doesn't damage his own interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, counsel, we will help as much as we can but it is primarily for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please tell us when -- if and when you want to go into private session and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last time around, you advised me that it would be better to have it in private session, so I'm going to heed that message and ask for a private session this time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that since there will be no session in this courtroom this afternoon and since we had a late start that we have a little bit more time than usual. I'm looking at the interpreters and they are nodding yes. Wherever the Chamber sometimes lacks flexibility, at least the interpreters and the technicians always show a level of flexibility, which is highly appreciated and admired. There is one remaining issue which is part of -- that is 16, the matters related to the accused's testimony. So apart from when and before Christmas or after Christmas but the issue of practicalities. I would like to see whether the parties have developed any opinion about that, such as communication with the then witness, although still being accused, and if there are any other matters. I don't know how the Defence understands the position to be once the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik would have started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We had assumed, Your Honour, that we would be unable to communicate with him but with this caveat that we suppose that if there were some practical matter that was really not related to his evidence, that we would approach the Prosecution and if necessary the Trial Chamber and we would seek appropriate clearance ad hoc to deal with that, Your Honour. That's what we had thought was the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had the same assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, since the parties do agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since the Chamber does not oppose to this approach, we don't have to discuss it at this very moment any more. If there would be at any time any other practical matter related to you, Mr. Stewart, and you, Mr. Josse, being counsel of both accused and witness at that time, then the Chamber would like to hear about it. But as far as communication is concerned, the approach adopted by both parties is supported by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn, as is said in good Latin, I think, sine die. I think the parties should be prepared to continue next Monday in the afternoon, the originally scheduled date. It has not been changed at this moment but the parties will be informed in advance of that. So that means not later than by tomorrow, whether we really expect them to appear at a quarter past 2 next Monday, the 27th of February, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: sine die. 23 24 25
